name: Hippocampus
function: The hippocampal formation curves along the medial floor of the temporal horn and includes hippocampus proper, dentate gyrus and subiculum in common usage. It participates in formation of new declarative memories and spatial/contextual representations through intrinsic circuits and distributed cortical/diencephalic networks. The whole structure is not a single nucleus.

afferent: Septal inputs through fornix and brainstem neuromodulation
efferent: Subicular/hippocampal output to entorhinal and wider association cortex
Fornix output to septal, mammillary and anterior thalamic targets

bloodSupply: Mainly PCA hippocampal branches with variable anterior choroidal contribution, especially anteriorly.

clinical.findings: Bilateral injury can cause severe impairment of new declarative learning; remote, working and procedural memory may be relatively preserved but outcomes vary. H.M. had bilateral medial temporal resections, not a selective hippocampal infarct.
Atrophy and signal changes may accompany mesial temporal epilepsy; sclerosis is not present in every case and does not by itself establish seizure onset.
Transient anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning may show delayed punctate hippocampal DWI lesions; this clinical syndrome is not synonymous with stroke or epilepsy.

name: Dentate gyrus
synonyms: dentate gyrus of the hippocampal formation
contextNote: A microscopic laminated hippocampal-field concept represented by an authored marker. The shape/coordinate does not establish CA/dentate/subicular boundaries; a host hippocampal mesh cannot independently validate a subfield segmentation. Named level membership is teaching/navigation metadata and has not been validated as a literal intersection of every displayed transverse section. The clinical text describes possible associations, not diagnostic rules.
function: The dentate gyrus is a folded, three-layered component of hippocampal formation with a granule-cell layer bordering the hilus. Entorhinal input reaches granule cells, whose mossy fibres project primarily to CA3. Experimental and human data support sparse coding/pattern separation; adult human neurogenesis has supporting evidence, while measured abundance and functional consequences remain method-dependent.

afferent: Predominantly entorhinal layer-II perforant input, with contributions from other layers
Local hilar/interneuron and septal modulatory inputs
efferent: Granule-cell mossy fibres to CA3 and local hilar circuits

bloodSupply: Shares hippocampal arterial territory, mainly PCA branches with variable anterior contribution.

clinical.findings: Granule-cell dispersion and mossy-fibre sprouting can occur, but neither finding alone proves the cause of seizures.
Dentate injury may affect encoding/discrimination within the wider hippocampal network; hemianopia requires separate visual-pathway injury.

name: Amygdala
function: The amygdala is a nuclear complex in the anterior medial temporal lobe, anterior/superior to the hippocampal head. Its basolateral, corticomedial and central groups participate in emotional salience, learning, motivation and autonomic responses through widespread networks. It is not a single fear center or the sole source of fear.

afferent: Olfactory, thalamic and brainstem visceral inputs, varying by nucleus
efferent: Stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal connections to basal forebrain/hypothalamus
Cortical, striatal, thalamic and brainstem connections, including central autonomic pathways

bloodSupply: Variable anterior choroidal, MCA temporal and PCA anterior temporal contributions.

clinical.findings: Can produce elements of Klüver-Bucy syndrome; the complete pattern usually involves broader temporal networks and is not obligatory after isolated amygdala damage.
Fear or autonomic auras can involve amygdala-centered networks, but these symptoms do not uniquely establish amygdala onset.
May impair recognition/learning of threat-related signals; preservation or loss of fear depends on stimulus and wider systems.

name: Fornix
function: The fornix is an arch-shaped hippocampal white-matter pathway formed from alveus/fimbria, crura, body and columns. Postcommissural fibres reach mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus; precommissural fibres reach septal/basal-forebrain targets. It also carries septohippocampal afferents, so it is not purely efferent.

afferent: Subiculum/hippocampal axons through alveus and fimbria
Septal cholinergic/GABAergic afferents traveling toward hippocampus
efferent: Mammillary bodies and direct anterior thalamic projections

bloodSupply: Small variable ACA/anterior communicating and choroidal-system branches along its course; no single vessel supplies the entire fornix.

clinical.findings: Bilateral injury can impair episodic memory; severity, recognition and recovery vary with lesion extent and associated damage.
Surgery or lesions near the foramen of Monro can injure fornices and impair memory; obstructive hydrocephalus is a distinct mechanism.

name: Commissure of the fornix
function: The hippocampal commissure lies between the fornical crura beneath the posterior corpus callosum and carries interhemispheric medial temporal connections. Human commissural organization differs from the much more prominent rodent ventral hippocampal commissure. It is distinct from the splenium.

afferent: Medial temporal/fornical commissural axons from both sides

bloodSupply: Small posterior/choroidal/pericallosal branches; precise human subregional territory is not independently mapped here.

clinical.findings: Commissural involvement may contribute to network dysfunction, but a specific isolated human syndrome is not established.
Alexia without agraphia classically involves dominant occipital and splenial pathways; it should not be assigned to hippocampal commissure alone.

name: Fimbria of the hippocampus
function: The fimbria is a white-matter fringe along the medial/superior hippocampal surface beside the choroidal fissure. Fibres from the alveus converge into it and continue posteriorly as the fornical crus. It carries hippocampal outputs and returning septal afferents.

efferent: Fornical crus/body/columns and their hippocampal/subcortical endpoints

bloodSupply: Shares variable hippocampal PCA/anterior choroidal arterial territory.

clinical.findings: Surgical or other medial temporal injury can disrupt memory networks; effects depend on side, bilaterality and accompanying hippocampal damage.
May involve fimbria together with hippocampal structures; visual field loss is not an intrinsic effect of fimbria injury.
